True wind Relative wind Ship
How it is calculated
  1. Relative wind is converted to a true bearing: ship's heading ± angle off the bow (+ Starboard, − Port).
  2. Relative wind and the ship's motion are each split into east and north components.
  3. Adding the ship's velocity to the relative wind leaves the true wind vector.
  4. True wind speed is the length of that vector. Its direction is shown as the bearing the wind blows from, with north written as 360°.
  5. Beaufort force and probable wave height (open sea) follow the WMO scale.

Same method as the “True Wind Calculation v 2.0” spreadsheet. For guidance only: always cross-check against the ship's instruments.

Choose the body, enter the time and your position to see the true azimuth and the working.
True azimuth
—
Altitude

How it is calculated
  1. UT is found from ship's time and LIT, or from the chronometer (CT ± CE) when one is entered.
  2. For a star: GHA of Aries for the hour plus the increment for the minutes and seconds, plus the star's SHA, gives the star's GHA. For the Sun, Moon and planets the GHA of the body is used directly.
  3. LHA = GHA + longitude east (or minus longitude west).
  4. A = tan Lat ÷ tan LHA, B = tan Dec ÷ sin LHA, C = A + B (add if the names are the same, subtract if different, named like the larger).
  5. Z = tan⁻¹ (1 ÷ (C × cos Lat)), named like C (N or S) and then E if LHA is more than 180°, otherwise W. Z is turned into a 000 – 360° true bearing.
  6. The result is checked against a direct calculation. The positions come from formulas accurate to about 0.1°, which is enough for a compass error. For a sextant fix use the Nautical Almanac.

Same method as the “True Azimuth” sheet of the Compass Error spreadsheet. For guidance only: cross-check against the Nautical Almanac when in doubt.

The rules behind it
  1. True bearing is the true azimuth of the body, worked by the A, B, C method and rounded to 0.1°.
  2. Gyro error = true bearing − gyro bearing. If the gyro reads less than true it is Low (East); if more, High (West).
  3. When the standard bearing is not read, it is taken as gyro bearing + (standard heading − gyro heading).
  4. Compass error = true bearing − compass bearing. Deviation = compass error − variation (East positive, West negative).
  5. The repeater side shows on which side of the ship's head the body lies, so you know which gyro repeater to use.
  6. The table of bodies uses the same positions: altitude and true azimuth for the date, GMT and position entered. Best bodies are stars at 15° – 30° altitude.

Same method as the “GYRO ERROR” sheet of the Compass Error spreadsheet. Positions are accurate to about 0.1°: enough for a compass error.

Working and how it is calculated
  1. Meridional parts: MP = 7915.7 log tan (45° + lat ÷ 2) − 23.3 sin lat, worked for each latitude.
  2. D.Lat = difference of latitude in minutes. D.Long = difference of longitude in minutes (the short way round, so a run across 180° is handled). DMP = difference of meridional parts.
  3. Course = tan⁻¹ (D.Long ÷ DMP), in the quadrant given by the signs. Distance = D.Lat ÷ cos course (D.Long × cos lat when the course is due east or west).
  4. Speed = distance ÷ time. The mid-latitude figures are a quick cross-check and agree closely on short runs.

Same method as the “Co's & Speed” sheet of the Compass Error spreadsheet. Distances are in nautical miles.

ETA table

Arrival in each destination's local time. Type the speeds in the table heading.

East of Greenwich is +, west is −. DTG is the distance to go in nautical miles.
How it is calculated
  1. Time to go = distance to go ÷ speed.
  2. The present time is turned into UTC with the time zone it is in, the time to go is added, and the result is turned into each destination's local time with that destination's time zone.
  3. Speeds not typed in are left out. A destination without a distance or a time zone is left blank.
  4. Weather, current and port traffic are not allowed for.

Same method as your ETA spreadsheets, with several destinations on one page.

Midship section

Upright position Square bilge corner used by the formula Below upright waterline

Heel shown to starboard; the result is the same to port. Freeboard and seabed are illustrative, not to scale.

Heeled draught table

Enter beam and draught to fill the table.

Understanding the calculation

Why heel makes the ship deeper

When a ship heels, she rotates about the waterline. One side lifts and the other goes down. The keel on the centreline actually rises slightly, but the bilge on the low side goes deeper than the upright keel. That corner of the hull is now the deepest point, so the ship needs more water than her upright draught suggests.

Wide ships feel this the most. On a ship with a 60 m beam, each 1° of heel adds roughly half a metre of draught. Heel can come from:

  • Turning: a ship heels outward in a turn, more so at higher speed.
  • Wind: steady beam wind pressure on the hull and superstructure.
  • A list: uneven cargo, ballast, bunkers or fresh water.
  • Rolling: in swell, the ship momentarily reaches her maximum roll angle.

In shallow water this extra draught comes straight out of your under-keel clearance (UKC).

The formula

Heeled draught = (½ × B × sin θ) + (d × cos θ)
Increase = Heeled draught − d

B = beam (m) · d = upright draught (m) · θ = angle of heel (degrees)

Where the formula comes from

Picture the hull cross-section as a rectangle (a “box-shaped” ship) that heels about the point where the centreline meets the waterline. The low-side bilge corner sits ½B out from the centreline and d below the waterline. When the box rotates through θ, that corner's depth below the waterline is made of two parts:

  • ½B × sin θ: the half-beam swinging downward. It is zero when upright and grows quickly as the ship heels.
  • d × cos θ: the upright draught, tilted over. It is a little less than d, because the ship's side is no longer vertical.

At small angles, sin θ grows much faster than cos θ shrinks, so the half-beam term dominates. That is why beam matters far more than draught here.

Worked example (using the values above)

    Note on radians: Excel's SIN and COS work in radians, which is why spreadsheets need a RADIANS column (degrees × π ÷ 180). This page converts for you, so always enter heel in degrees.

    Quick mental check

    For small angles (up to about 5°), the increase is roughly B × 0.0087 for each degree of heel. That is ½B × π/180. A 60 m beam gives about 0.52 m per degree, and a 32 m beam about 0.28 m per degree. Use it to sanity-check any figure you are given.

    Assumptions and limits

    • Box-shaped section. Real ships have a rounded bilge, so the true increase is slightly less than calculated. The answer errs on the safe side.
    • Use the full beam and the deepest draught for a quick, conservative figure. If the ship is trimmed, the deepest point is at one end, where the hull is narrower, so the real increase there is smaller.
    • Heel only. It does not include squat, wave or swell motion, or changes in water density. Allow for these separately.
    • Valid while the low-side deck edge stays out of the water and the high-side bilge stays in it. That is far beyond normal heel angles for a loaded ship.

    Using it for under-keel clearance

    UKC = (charted depth + height of tide) − (heeled draught + squat)

    Compare the result with the minimum UKC required by your company's SMS, the charterer, or the port or pilotage authority for that passage. When planning, use the largest heel you can reasonably expect: the turn rate and speed through bends, the forecast wind, and any list.

    Heeled draught—

    Formula: Heeled draught = (½ × B × sin θ) + (d × cos θ); Increase = Heeled draught − d. A box-shaped section is assumed, so the real increase is slightly less (safe side). Heel only: add squat and other allowances separately when calculating under-keel clearance.

    Max deck to seabed
    —
    Max depth of water
    —

    Limit condition: anchor just clear of the seabed

    Anchor cable Kenter joining shackle between shackles

    Shackles are counted from the anchor: the 1st shackle is joined to the anchor. At this depth the windlass is lifting the anchor and every shackle hanging below the deck. Not to scale horizontally.

    Calculation sheet

    Understanding the calculation

    Why there is a depth limit

    When you heave up, the moment the anchor leaves the seabed the windlass is holding the anchor plus every metre of cable hanging between the deck and the anchor. The deeper the water, the longer that hanging cable, and the heavier the load.

    If that load is more than the windlass can pull, the anchor cannot be recovered. The motor or hydraulics may stall or be damaged, the brake may be overloaded, and the anchor and cable can be lost.

    The calculation

    Hanging weight to start = anchor + joining shackle + 1st shackle
    Usable pull = windlass capacity × (1 − allowance)
    Spare pull = usable pull − hanging weight to start
    Further shackles = spare pull ÷ weight of 1 shackle
    Deck to seabed = (1 + further shackles) × 27.5 m
    Depth of water = deck to seabed − deck height above WL

    Worked example (using the values above)

      Why the 20 % allowance

      The windlass's rated pull is what it delivers at the gypsy. Part of it is lost to friction as the cable runs through the hawse pipe and over the gypsy, and an older windlass may no longer reach its rated figure. The sheet deducts 20 % for this; change it if your SMS uses a different figure.

      Class rules size the windlass assuming the hawse pipe is 70 % efficient and the weights are in seawater. Taking the weights in air with a 20 % allowance gives almost exactly the same answer (0.80 against 0.805 of the rated pull). So this method matches the class basis: the result is a limit, not a figure with extra margin built in.

      Deck to seabed vs depth of water

      The sheet's answer is the length of cable from the deck to the anchor, so it is measured from the deck. The chart gives depth from the sea surface. Subtract the height of the forecastle deck above the waterline to get the depth of water you can safely anchor in.

      That height changes with draught and trim, and it is much greater in ballast. Use the depth of water at the highest tide expected while at anchor, since that is when the most cable will hang when you heave up.

      Assumptions and limits

      • Weights in air. Steel weighs about 13 % less in seawater, but that roughly cancels the extra hawse-pipe friction class assumes (30 % rather than 20 %). Treat the answer as the limit, with no hidden margin.
      • Cable hanging vertically with the anchor just clear of the bottom: the worst moment of heaving up.
      • Measured from the deck. The gypsy sits above the deck and the cable runs down the hawse pipe, so slightly more cable hangs than the deck-to-seabed figure. Keep a few metres in hand.
      • Breaking out. Class requires a short-term pull of 1.5 × the continuous pull for 2 minutes to break the anchor out, but do not rely on it. Heave only when the cable is up and down and use the engine to bring the ship over the anchor; never use the windlass to drag the ship.
      • Whole shackles. In practice round the result down to whole shackles, as shown under the result.

      What class rules say (IACS UR A3)

      IACS UR A3, Anchor Windlass Design and Testing (2017, Rev.1 2019; earlier editions of UR A1 had similar requirements), requires the windlass to give a continuous duty pull for at least 30 minutes. For Grade 3 cable this is 4.84 × d² kgf, with d the cable diameter in mm. For 114 mm cable that is 62.9 t, which matches the figure in the DHT LEOPARD sheet.

      That rated pull is for an anchorage depth down to 82.5 m (3 shackles); deeper anchorages need a windlass with a higher rated pull. The mean hoisting speed must be at least 0.15 m/s (9 m/min), measured over two shackles starting with three shackles and the anchor hanging free. That is why the capacity is quoted “@ 9 m/min”.

      Windlasses certified from July 2018 are marked with their maximum anchorage depth. Enter it, or the maker's figure, as the rated anchorage depth. If it is less than the calculated depth, the lower figure governs.

      Deep-water anchoring

      P&I clubs and DNV report many anchors lost in deep anchorages, often when several shackles were walked out and the rest let go on the brake, which could not stop the run-out. In deep water, walk the anchor out under power all the way to the seabed, check the windlass and brake are in good order beforehand, and follow your SMS anchoring procedure.

      Max deck to seabed—
      Max depth of water—

      Method: usable pull = windlass continuous duty pull less the allowance for friction and age (20 % with weights in air ≈ the IACS UR A3 basis of 70 % hawse-pipe efficiency with weights in seawater). The pull left after lifting the anchor, joining shackle and 1st shackle, divided by the weight of one shackle, gives the further shackles that can be lifted. Do not exceed the windlass's rated anchorage depth. Breaking out is not included. Use the depth of water at the highest expected tide.

      How it is worked, and how accurate it is
      1. The Sun's position is computed for each moment (about 0.003° accuracy) and the moment its altitude reaches the target is found to the second, at your own position. The result is rounded to the nearest minute (some websites cut the seconds off instead, so they can show a minute less).
      2. Sunrise and sunset are when the Sun's upper limb is on the horizon: centre at −(34′ refraction + 16′ semi-diameter), about −0°50′. This is the Nautical Almanac rule.
      3. Twilight: civil begins and ends with the Sun's centre at −6°, nautical at −12° (the time for star sights, when the horizon and the stars are both visible), astronomical at −18°.
      4. Height of eye lowers the horizon by the dip, 1.76 × √height (arc minutes), so the Sun appears earlier and disappears later.
      5. Ship's time = UTC + zone. LMT = UTC + longitude ÷ 15.
      6. Checked against a full planetary ephemeris at 420+ events from 60°S to 66°N: the largest difference was 11 seconds. Real refraction depends on temperature and pressure, so allow about a minute for the weather, more near the poles.
      7. Moonrise and moonset are when the Moon's upper limb is on the horizon, worked from your own position (so the Moon's large parallax is included) with the same Moon used for Moon sights. Checked against JPL DE440.
      8. Under way: give course, speed and the ship's time of the position. Each event is then worked at the position the ship will be in at that moment, so a fast ship running east sees the Sun rise earlier than at anchor.
      9. Near the poles the Sun may not rise or set, or twilight may not end: the table says so instead of showing a time.

      Maritime security charts: limits

      Admiralty Q charts show piracy and security areas, reporting schemes and transit corridors. These six are the whole series. Q6113 is now titled Andaman Islands to the Torres Strait, including Indonesia: check its latest edition.

      Design System

      iMariners Bridge Calculators, version 1.0. The one place that defines colour, type, spacing and components. Every tool reads from it, so nothing changes from tab to tab.

      Art direction: the chart table

      Bridge Calculators should feel like instruments on a chart table: calm, exact, readable at 3 a.m. under a red light. Every tool is a page of the same product.

      One idea

      • Navy console on the left holds the iMariners logo and the tools. It is the instrument frame.
      • White cards on chart paper are the work sheets. A faint chart grid sits behind them.
      • Teal is the brand and the only action colour. Amber marks a cell you type into.
      • Red and green keep their seafaring meaning: port and starboard, avoid and take, west and east.
      • Night mode is red only. Dusk is the same layout in dark blue.

      Every page has the same parts

      1. Sidebar: the logo, five groups, one line per tool, a bar on the page you are on.
      2. Top bar: where you are, the Saved mark, the ship, Day / Dusk / Night.
      3. Page header: title, one sentence, and the ruler of tick marks.
      4. Cards: small mono capital title with a teal square, then the content.
      5. Width: one content width and one left edge on every page.

      Brand

      On the sidebar (white wordmark version)
      On white: documents, print, other websites (teal version)
      • Two versions only: the white wordmark on navy (sidebar) and the teal original on white. Never stretch, recolour or add a box behind it. Night mode tints the sidebar one red automatically.
      • Keep clear space equal to the height of the "i" around it. Minimum height 24 px on screen.
      • The product name sits beside it in regular type, separated by a thin rule: iMariners | Bridge Calculators.

      Page patterns

      A tool page

      Every tool is one <section class="tool" id="..."> with the same four parts, in this order.

      1. .tool-head: one h1 and one sentence saying what the tool is for.
      2. .grid or .tool-layout: inputs card on the left, results on the right. Wide tables take the full row.
      3. .card: every block of content. Card titles are small caps h2.
      4. .explain: optional "how it is calculated" below.

      Adding a new tool

      1. Copy the section skeleton above into <main> and add its link to the side navigation, under the right heading.
      2. Write initYourTool() and add it to the TOOLS list.
      3. Save inputs with store.get / store.set under a bridgeCalc. key, so it is included in the optional backup on the Ship Particulars page.
      4. Use only tokens from this page. If something is missing, add the token here first, in all three themes.
      5. Check it in Day, Dusk and Night, and on a phone width.

      Fields and spacing helpers

      Every field you type into looks the same: --input-bg background, hairline border, teal focus ring, red border when invalid. Cells in tables where you enter data use the warm --entry tint, so "type here" is always the same colour. Tools only change the size.

      --entry: a cell you type into--input-bg: a plain field

      Spacing helpers for markup (never write px inline): u-mt-0 u-mt-1 u-mt-1h u-mt-2h u-mt-3 u-mt-3h u-mt-4 u-mt-5 u-mb-0 u-list u-sub u-center u-right.

      Compliance check

      Scans this page's own stylesheet for anything that bypasses the system: colour codes, font names, pixel font sizes, pixel corner radii. Print sheets and the theme definitions are exempt. Run it after adding or changing a tool.
